prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: separating joint policyholders after a break-up. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When joint policyholders have separated, confirm who is occupying or keeping each insured property before making any triage decision, because cover and next steps can differ once one person has moved out."},{"type":"fact","content":"When one policyholder asks to deal with the claim alone, check whether the other named policyholder must still be included for consent, instructions or payment authority, especially where both names remain on the policy."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the breakup is recent, expect contact details, access arrangements and possession of keys to be unsettled, so I verify the safest single point of contact before arranging inspections or collections."},{"type":"preference","content":"When policyholders disagree, I prefer to pause non-urgent settlement steps and record the dispute clearly, rather than risk paying the wrong party or sending a repairer to the wrong place."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a joint home policy is tied to a shared property but only one person remains there, I check whether they have the legal right to act for the insured premises, because occupation alone may not be enough."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a motor claim follows a separation, I always confirm who usually drives, who has the vehicle, and whether any change in keeper, address or named drivers has happened since the break-up."},{"type":"fact","content":"When repair authorisation depends on consent, I treat absent joint policyholders as still relevant unless the policy or evidence shows one person now has sole authority."},{"type":"observation","content":"When emotions are running high, short and neutral wording works best; I avoid repeating the relationship history and focus on practical questions about property, ownership and safe access."},{"type":"preference","content":"When there is a risk of duplicate claims or conflicting instructions, I prefer one documented timeline of events from both parties, even if it means asking for the same facts in a structured way."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the separation affects cover mid-claim, I check whether addresses, vehicles, valuables or temporary accommodation arrangements need to be updated, because the claim facts may no longer match the policy records."}]}
